newsitem.title: USA: Golf-Norman turning the page on worst chapter at Masters.
newsitem.headline: Golf-Norman turning the page on worst chapter at Masters.

text.p: Greg Norman is finally ready to turn the page on the worst chapter of his estimable golf career, armed with a renewed belief in himself after a marathon session with a motivational guru.

Norman, arriving at Augusta National on Tuesday, said the story of his final-round collapse at the Masters last year was a dead issue from this day on and gave thanks to motivational speaker Tony Robbins for pointing him in the right direction.
"I gave you a pretty good story to write this past year and I hope to give you another story, a better one to write about," Norman, 42, told a news conference.

The Australian went into the final round last year with a six-shot lead over Nick Faldo and the title he yearns for most within easy reach. By day's end, he had suffered the worst collapse in a major championship, shooting 78 to lose by five.
Norman, who in years past has sought strength from zen philosophy to help him deal with disappointing defeats, said "a wonderful session" with Roberts Monday had turned him around.
"We could all do with flushing the toilet every couple of years and getting the crap out of your head. You just sometimes sit down and pull the chain. We all fall into the same trap," he said.
"It was a case of reminding myself of who I am and how good I am. I know these things from 21 years in golf. I know these things. I was re-educating myself, that was all I was doing."
Robbins, star of late-night cable television motivational programmes and seminars around the country, spurs audiences to feel good and positive as a means of succeeding in business and in life.
Norman, who has made a separate fortune off the course with his business dealings, said his day spent with Robbins was just the tonic he needed to shed the memory of his last visit here.
"Last year was the worst round of my life," said Norman, who blamed himself for stubbornly pushing ever harder to make things happen despite a flaw in his swing.
"I push myself everywhere," Norman continued. "On the golf course, in business. I'm amazed I even survived a year the way I push myself.
"The intensity -- I went from the practice, office, gym, go to bed. Practice, office, gym. I was so regimented in doing what I was doing, that I forgot the good things in life."
Norman said it didn't take him long to get over the immediate pain from the last Masters' Sunday, but it took time to find renewal.
"I had a bad day Monday," said Norman, who sat in the plane for an hour and a half Sunday night before disembarking upon returning home to Florida from the Augusta debacle.
"Tuesday morning I was hung over like hell. But by Tuesday lunch I was all right."
Norman said Robbins had helped him get back into the habits that have helped bring out his best in the past.

"It's like talking to yourself in a mirror," he said. "You hear yourself telling yourself what you've done and how good you are. It's just positive reinforcement. I hadn't done that in a couple of years. You get lazy.
"We all fall into the same trap. We all get in the car every day and ride to work the same way every day. All of a sudden there's a detour in the road and you're lost."
Not even a two-hour-long traffic jam that delayed his arrival at Augusta National nettled Norman.
"Even my wife says to me, 'I am so proud of you; you never even raised your voice or whacked the dashboard or anything,'" he said with a grin.
Still, the proud Australian, winner of two British Opens and a passel of tournaments around the world, said he would not change his aggressive golf game.

"Looking back over the 79 victories that I've had, I've played the way I want to play. If my mind tells me to aim it 15 feet to the right of the hole, I would. If I feel I should take a 3-wood and hit it wherever, I'll do it, because I've done it my entire life.
"You're not going to be Mr. Perfect from here on in. But if you do it your way, you accept it a lot easier."
